dataset.description: In this project, no work involves human participants, personal data, human cells or tissues, animals, non‑EU countries, artificial intelligence, or any activity that could generate dual‑use concerns. The only ethical dimension relates to the project’s interaction with the natural environment, specifically the temporary installation of non‑destructive sensors and benthic chambers in seagrass meadows and the collection of a small number of seagrass shoots for biomass measurements. The project follows the “Do No Harm” principle, applying strict safeguards to avoid ecological disturbance in protected habitats. All deployments use established, non‑invasive techniques that have repeatedly shown no detectable impact on seagrass structure, sediment stability, or ecosystem functioning. Biomass sampling is minimal, spatially distributed, and far below thresholds known to affect meadow integrity. The project is adherent to responsible research practices, including environmental stewardship, transparency, open science, and compliance with institutional safety procedures. No intellectual property is expected to arise from the work, and all research outputs will be openly shared.

format:
The project will generate a wide range of environmental, biogeochemical, and analytical data derived from field incubations, laboratory analyses, and subsequent data processing. No external datasets will be reused beyond standard environmental baselines or climate projections already publicly available.

1. Field Data (raw and processed)
Collected during benthic chamber incubations and multiparameter sensor deployments in seagrass meadows.
Benthic chamber time‑series measurements of:
  • DIC, TA, pH
  • Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O)
  • Nutrients (PO₄, NH₄, NO₃, NO₂, SiO₂)
  • PIC, POC, DIC in sediments and water
  • Chlorophyll
Format: CSV, XLSX, instrument‑generated text files (e.g., .txt, .dat)

Multiparameter sensor data (temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen, irradiance, pH)
Format: CSV, TXT, proprietary sensor exports

Field metadata (GPS coordinates, deployment logs, environmental notes)
Format: CSV, TXT, PDF

2. Laboratory Analytical Data
Generated at Kristineberg’s accredited facilities.
  • Picarro GHG analyser outputs (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O), Format: CSV, TXT, proprietary instrument files
  • Spectrophotometric pH and total alkalinity titration data, Format: CSV, XLSX
  • Nutrient concentrations from SWEDAC‑accredited labs, Format: PDF reports, CSV, XLSX
  • Carbonate chemistry measurements (PIC, POC, DIC), Format: CSV, XLSX
3. Derived and Processed Data
Generated during data analysis
  • Flux calculations (DIC, TA, GHGs, nutrients, carbon pools), Format: CSV, XLSX, RDS
  • Carbonate system parameters computed using seacarb, Format: CSV, RDS
  • Statistical outputs (regressions, factorial analyses, descriptive statistics), Format: CSV tables, R scripts (.R), R Markdown (.Rmd)
  • Figures and visualisations, Format: PNG, PDF
4. Documentation and Metadata
  • Sampling protocols, chamber deployment logs, laboratory protocols
  • Data dictionaries, README files, variable definitions, units
  • Workflow documentation and codebooks
Format: PDF, TXT, DOCX, Markdown (.md)

dmp.description: Seagrass ecosystems are considered key blue carbon sinks due to their capacity to store particulate organic carbon in the sediments. However, other mechanisms of carbon sequestration remain understudied, such as outwelling or export of recalcitrant dissolved carbon. This project aims to unravel these pathways through the study of how theseecosystems influence the seawater carbonate system in present and future climatic conditions. Using advanced instrumentation at Kristineberg Centre—Picarro gas analysers, automatic alkalinity titrators, spectrophotometers, and nutrient analysis facilities— together with in situ field measurements in nearby meadows; the study will assess fluxes of multiple carbon species and greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O). Results will determine whether these ecosystems act as carbon sinks or sources. Expected outcomes include improved understanding of the role of seagrasses in coastal carbon budgets and guidance for their inclusion in climate mitigation strategies.
